name: White Tai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gedney, William J. 1989 [1964]. A comparative sketch of White, Black and Red Tai. In Robert J. Bickner, John Hartmann, Thomas John Hudak & Patcharin Peyasantiwong (eds.), Selected papers on comparative Tai studies (Michigan Papers on South and Southeast Asia 29), 415-461. Ann Arbor: Center for South and Southeast Asian Studies, University of Michigan. [orig. Social Science Review (Bangkok), special number, 14 December 1964: 1-47]
catalog_locator: p. 421 (1989 reprint pagination), paragraph after 'On checked syllables Red Tai has', immediately before the heading COMPARISON OF TONES. Checked on the page scan (page numbered 421 at foot); tone inventory p. 419; isolation-form statement p. 418.
catalog_quote: All the languages dealt with here (W B R S) have, in addition to the types of syllables already described, other syllables having weak stress, usually prefixed to a normal syllable. Such weak syllables usually have a short a vowel, though sometimes other vowels occur. The tone on such syllables tends to be neutralized to a mid level pitch in all four languages. Though this phenomenon would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language, it is so infrequent in the type of words that we are dealing with that we can get along by the simple device of placing a short mark ˘ over the vowel; if we know from slower pronunciation what the reduced tone would have been, we will mark it, for example S măphraaw4 or mă4phraaw4 'coconut.' It is noteworthy that of the four languages here studied, Siamese has by far the greatest number of such weak syllables, Red Tai somewhat fewer, Black Tai still fewer, and in White Tai they are infrequent. This order coincides with the relative geographical location of the languages.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tai Dón is a six-tone language whose words are essentially monosyllabic tone-bearing ('normal') syllables. The only stress statement is that a minor class of weakly stressed syllables (short a vowel, tone neutralised to mid level) can be prefixed to a normal syllable, i.e. in the rare sesquisyllabic words the final (main) syllable carries full stress and tone and the presyllable is weak; such words are infrequent in White Tai. No stress rule is stated for monosyllables or for compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the only stress distinction drawn is weak (presyllable) vs normal syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak syllables 'usually' have short a; 'sometimes other vowels occur'; Gedney says the phenomenon 'would have to be dealt with in a more thorough analysis of each language' and marks such syllables only with a breve.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic word shapes) in citation forms from Gedney's 1964 field notes; a comparative sketch of four languages, not a description of Tai Dón word stress as such. White Tai data = Lai Châu (muang lay) and Muong Te speakers at Tung Nghia.
new_statements.identity_note: Gedney's 'White Tai' = the speech of Lai Châu (muang lay) and Muong Te (muang te) people recorded at the Tung Nghia refugee settlement near Dalat in July 1964 = Tai Dón proper (taid1250). Minot 1940 and Martini 1954 likewise describe the Lai Châu / Muong Te / Phong Thổ variety. Caution on two Glottolog-listed references: Savina 1910 and Bonifacy 1907 describe the Tày of the Clear River, which Gedney (p. 416) explicitly separates from White Tai ('differ greatly in initial consonants'); they belong to Tày (tayy1240 / tyz) rather than taid1250.

new_statements.quote: 1.5 Emphatic stress. A slight lengthening of the syllable utterance final is normal. Emphatic stress consists of extra loudness and of lengthening of the vowel and the final sonorant, if there is one; it occurs on syllables utterance finally or medially. On the mid-low and mid tones the pitch may be slightly higher than normally. [...] The preceding remarks are based on very limited occurrences of the phenomena in my tapes. Further study will be required to confirm the observations made thus far and to make possible a detailed description of stress, intonation, and juncture. || p. 5: The syllable structure in White Tai is identical with its morpheme structure. Only six two-syllable items have been observed in which neither syllable could be identified as a morpheme.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's only statement (Gedney 1964 p. 421: tone language; weak-stressed short-a presyllables exist but 'in White Tai they are infrequent'). Donaldson 1963, on the same Lai Chau/Tung Nghia speech, adds that morphemes are monosyllabic (near-absence of presyllabic structure), that utterance-final syllables are slightly lengthened, and that stress is otherwise only emphatic/utterance-level with tone-allophone effects; it gives no word-level placement rule and does not contradict Gedney.
new_statements.rule_in_words: White Tai (Lai Chau) is analysed as a seven-tone language whose syllable equals the morpheme (only six unanalysable disyllables noted); the only stress the thesis describes is emphatic stress, an utterance-level phenomenon (extra loudness plus lengthening of vowel and final sonorant, with raised pitch allophones of several tones), occurring on utterance-final or medial syllables; utterance-final syllables are normally slightly lengthened. No lexical/word-stress placement rule is given, and the author says a description of stress, intonation and juncture awaits further study.
new_statements.exceptions: Low glottal tone not yet observed under emphatic stress; high glottal keeps its glottal stop under emphasis while mid glottal loses it; the emphasised syllable (or its phrase) may be repeated. Six two-syllable items (footnote p. 5, e.g. 'spider', 'vinegar', si-so 'to rub') are the only non-monomorphemic disyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Donaldson 1963 and 1976 both rest on Lai Châu (Muong Lay) White Tai speakers resettled at Tung Nghia near Dalat, 1960-61, i.e. Tai Dón proper, the same community Gedney recorded in 1964. Savina 1910's 'Tày' is identified by Donaldson 1963 (p. 2, following Li 1959/1960) as a Central Tai dialect and by Gedney 1964 (p. 416) as an eastern/northeastern variety 'also sometimes called White Tai' with very different initials: not this language.
